title: Halide Perovskite Photocatalysts for Hydrogen Production from Hydrogen Halide Splitting: Progress, Stability and the Lead-Toxicity Challenge
content: Purpose Photocatalytic splitting of hydrogen halides (HX; X = I, Br) over halide perovskites has moved from 0.81% solar-to-hydrogen (STH) efficiency in 2017 to reported values above 5% within a decade. The field rests on one idea: in a saturated HX solution, a soluble perovskite sits in dynamic equilibrium with its dissolved ions and therefore persists in an aqueous medium. This review covers the principles of that equilibrium, lead-based perovskites, co-catalysts including single atoms, and lead-free bismuth, tin, antimony and double perovskites, and asks whether reported performance can be compared. Methods In this critical narrative review, 24 experimental HX-splitting studies were analysed in full; reaction conditions, rates, efficiencies, sacrificial reagents, stability and lead-related observations were extracted manually and compared. Results Most studies use hypophosphorous acid (H3PO2) as a sacrificial reductant, rates are normalised in incompatible ways, and ten of twelve lead-free studies report no STH-type efficiency. In the only direct comparison, removing H3PO2 lowered the STH of one system from 3.85% to an initial 1.02%, reflecting both the loss of the sacrificial electron donor and light shielding by accumulating triiodide, so H3PO2-assisted values are not HX-splitting efficiencies. Lead accounting is largely missing: metallic Pb formation and hydrogen evolved from photocorrosion are rarely separated from true HX splitting. Conclusion Reported performance is not yet comparable across studies. We propose a minimum reporting set for HX splitting, a lead-accounting protocol, and a route map for using the halogen product, from I3−/I− recycling for overall water splitting to coupling with hydrogen sulfide treatment.
